metodo.sub: Two frameworks in sequence: first the DIAGNOSIS of how the failure behaves over time, then the PRESCRIPTION of the task. That is how every failure mode in the collection is treated — and how the selector below decides.
metodo.aResumo: How the failure behaves over time: Nowlan & Heap pattern and Weibull β.
metodo.bResumo: The applicable and effective task: CBM, TBM, Proof Test, RTF — or redesign.

fwA.sub: How the failure behaves over time
fwA.p1: Before deciding what to do about a failure, you need to know how it happens over time. Framework A answers exactly that: does the failure mode age (wear-out), is it random, or is it most likely right after an intervention (infant mortality)?
fwA.nhP1: The classic Nowlan & Heap study (United Airlines, 1978) measured conditional probability of failure against age for thousands of items and found six patterns — with the result that redefined maintenance: only ~11% of items (patterns A, B and C) show a clear wear-out zone that justifies age-based intervention. The other ~89% are dominated by randomness or infant mortality — where scheduled overhaul does not help and can make things worse.
fwA.betaP1: The shape parameter β of the Weibull distribution turns the pattern into a number: β < 1 = infant mortality; β ≈ 1 = random (constant rate); β > 1 = wear-out. Every failure-mode note in the collection carries this reading in the purple Framework A panel — with the editorial category and the typical β cited in the literature.
fwA.betaCalc: Explore it in the Weibull calculator →
fwA.saidaP1: The output of Framework A is the input of Framework B: only after knowing whether the failure gives a measurable warning (P-F interval), whether it ages and whether operations can see it does choosing the task make sense.
fwA.irSeletor: Apply it in the strategy selector →
fwA.exemplo: Real example in the collection: Cavitation →

fwB.p1: With the diagnosis in hand, Framework B decides what to do — in the RCM order of preference (SAE JA1011; Moubray, RCM II). A task only enters the plan if it is technically APPLICABLE (detects or prevents that failure mode) and WORTH DOING (costs less than the consequence it avoids).
fwB.hierCbm: On-condition — if the failure gives a measurable warning (P-F interval), monitor the condition and act on the signal. Inspection ≤ P-F/2.
fwB.hierTbm: Scheduled restoration/discard — only when a defined wear-out zone exists (β > 1 with predictable age). Interval before the wear zone.
fwB.hierProof: Failure-finding — for HIDDEN functions (protections, redundancies): tests the function at the interval (FFI) dictated by the required availability.
fwB.hierRtf: Run to failure — legitimate when nothing above applies and the consequence is economic only.
fwB.hierRedesenho: Redesign — compulsory when the consequence is safety/environmental and no task reduces the risk to a tolerable level.
fwB.consP1: The same technical failure changes strategy with its consequence: safety/environmental demands proven risk reduction (or redesign); operational weighs downtime cost; non-operational weighs repair cost only. That is why the selector asks about consequence before closing the decision.
fwB.acervoP1: Every failure-mode note publishes with its Framework B decision and an exportable maintenance plan (green panel) — coherence enforced at build time: CBM requires a P-F interval, proof testing requires a hidden failure, RTF requires no P-F.
fwB.irSeletor: Apply it in the strategy selector →
fwB.exemplo: Real example in the collection: the Cavitation plan →

seletor.intro: Which maintenance strategy is best for my asset, given the failure mode I do not want to happen? Answer the 4 questions — the RCM decision diagram returns the strategy and the base plan. Everything runs in your browser: no data leaves this page.
seletor.q1: 1 · How does the failure behave over time? (Framework A)
seletor.q1_infantil: Infant mortality — most likely right after installation or intervention (β < 1)
seletor.q1_aleatoria: Random — constant rate, does not age (β ≈ 1)
seletor.q1_desgaste: Wear-out — ages, with predictable failure age (β > 1)
seletor.q2: 2 · Is the failure evident to operations?
seletor.q2Hint: Under normal conditions, does anyone notice the failure occurred (alarm, visible loss of function)? Protections and redundancies are usually hidden.
seletor.q3: 3 · Is there a measurable warning before failure (P-F interval)?
seletor.q3Hint: Vibration, temperature, thickness, noise, process trend — something that leaves time to act between the signal (P) and functional failure (F).
seletor.q3_nao: No — or the window is unworkable
seletor.q4: 4 · What is the worst plausible consequence?

periodicidades.pf_metade: ≤ half the P-F interval (Moubray, RCM II, ch. 8)
periodicidades.fracao_vida: before the wear zone — e.g. ≤ B10 life (Weibull)

avisos.seguranca_reduzir_risco: Safety consequence: the task must demonstrably reduce the risk to a tolerable level — otherwise combine tasks or redesign.
avisos.proof_test_seguranca_redesenho: Protection with a safety consequence: if the test interval cannot deliver the required availability, redesign is compulsory (SAE JA1011).
avisos.redesenho_compulsorio: With no applicable proactive task and a safety consequence, RCM does not accept living with the risk: a design change is mandatory.
avisos.rtf_operacional_reavaliar: RTF with relevant downtime cost: reconsider redesign or redundancy if the cost of stopping exceeds the cost of prevention.
avisos.infantil_causa_raiz: β < 1: scheduled intervention INTRODUCES failures (Nowlan & Heap). Attack the root cause — commissioning, assembly, quality — instead of overhauling by age.

guia.sub: The theory behind the three tools, what each parameter actually is, where the numbers come from and how to read the results. Not everyone carries this by heart — that is what this guide is for.
guia.fluxoTexto: The three calculators answer the method's three quantitative questions: Weibull reads HOW the failure behaves over time (Framework A); MTBF·MTTR·Availability measure the IMPACT of failure and repair; and the P-F interval sizes the INSPECTION when the strategy is on-condition (Framework B).
guia.ondeTexto: The raw material is your maintenance history (CMMS/SAP-PM/Maximo): failure dates, operating hours and repair times — always PER FAILURE MODE. Mixing different failure modes in one sample is the number-one analysis mistake. Without enough history, use typical values from the literature (the collection's notes cite the typical β and P-F of each failure mode) or industry databases (e.g. OREDA for oil & gas).

weibull.teoria: The Weibull distribution is reliability's Swiss-army knife because a single shape parameter (β) reproduces all three failure regimes. Reliability is R(t) = exp(−(t/η)^β) — the probability that the item reaches age t alive. The instantaneous failure rate is h(t) = (β/η)·(t/η)^(β−1).
weibull.parametros: β (beta, shape parameter) — reads the failure pattern: β < 1 = infant mortality (failure rate FALLS with time — the danger is early life); β ≈ 1 = random (constant rate — the item does not age; age does not predict failure); β > 1 = wear-out (rate RISES with age — a wear zone exists). η (eta, characteristic life) — the age by which 63.2% of the population has failed, whatever the β; it is the curve's scale factor. t (mission time) — the horizon you want to assess (e.g. the campaign until the next shutdown).
weibull.estimar: Collect times-to-failure of the SAME failure mode (practical minimum: 5–7 failures). Items that have not failed or were preventively replaced enter as suspensions (censoring) — ignoring them distorts β. Estimation: Weibull paper / median-rank regression or maximum likelihood (spreadsheets and reliability software do this). Without your own data: start from the typical β cited in the literature and in the collection's notes and calibrate η with the average life observed at your plant.
weibull.usar: Enter β and η (and the mission t in the sliders). Read: MTTF — the mean life = η·Γ(1+1/β); B10 — the age by which 10% of the population fails (the classic bearing-selection criterion); R(t) and h(t) at the mission time; and the automatic Fw A reading (the diagnostic category that feeds the strategy selector).

disp.titulo: 2 · MTBF · MTTR · Availability — measuring the impact
disp.teoria: For repairable items the cycle is operate → fail → repair → operate. Inherent availability Ai = MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR) is the fraction of time the asset is fit for duty, considering only the technical repair time (no logistics, spares or waiting). It is the design ruler — the operational availability measured in the field will always be lower.
disp.parametros: MTBF (mean time BETWEEN failures — repairable items) — operating hours ÷ number of failures in the period. Use OPERATING hours, not calendar hours: an asset running 60% of the time 'ages' 60%. MTTR (mean time to repair) — sum of restoration times ÷ number of repairs, from start of intervention to return in fit condition.
disp.estimar: Both come straight from the CMMS; 12–24 month windows give reasonable samples. Classic traps: counting preventive work as failure (it is not), missing the 'small' failures fixed by operations without a work order, and mixing failure modes with different dynamics into one MTBF.
disp.usar: Enter MTBF and MTTR. Read Ai (in %) and the annual unavailability over 8,760 h — the number management understands: expected downtime hours per year for this failure+repair pair.

pf.teoria: Between point P (the failure becomes DETECTABLE: vibration rises, temperature shifts, thickness drops) and point F (the function is lost) there is a window — the P-F interval. An on-condition task is only effective if the inspection fits INSIDE that window; consecrated practice is to inspect every P-F/2, guaranteeing at least two detection chances before F (Moubray, RCM II, ch. 8).
pf.parametros: P-F interval — the typical time between the first detectable symptom and functional failure. Note: it depends on the failure mode AND the detection TECHNIQUE — for the same bearing, ultrasound/enveloping sees it earlier (larger P-F) than the vibration spectrum, which sees it earlier than temperature or audible noise. Inspection interval — the periodicity your route practices today (weekly, monthly…).
pf.estimar: Three sources, in this order: your own historical cases (time between first alarm and failure in the events that 'escaped' the route); the experience of the plant's condition-monitoring specialists; the technique's literature — the collection's failure-mode notes carry the cited typical P-F. When in doubt, be conservative: assume the smaller P-F.
pf.usar: Enter the P-F interval and the practiced inspection interval (any unit — days, weeks — as long as it is the same in both). Read the recommended value (P-F/2), how many detection chances your route gives inside the window, the remaining margin and the adequate / review verdict.

guia.fontes: Guide references: Smith — Reliability, Maintainability and Risk (2004) · Moubray — RCM II (1997), ch. 8 · Nowlan & Heap (1978). The full theory of the two frameworks lives in The method.

weibull.invalido: Invalid inputs: β and η must be positive.
weibull.rodape: R(t) = exp(−(t/η)^β) · h(t) = (β/η)·(t/η)^(β−1). Validated against Smith (2004) and known properties (R(η)=e⁻¹). The note's editorial category prevails over this didactic reading.

disp.rodape: Ai = MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR) — inherent availability (Smith 2004, ch. 2). Reference year: 8760 h.

pf.rodape: An on-condition task is only effective if inspection fits the P-F window — consecrated practice: inspection ≤ P-F/2 (Moubray, RCM II ch. 8).

busca.dica: Try broader terms — e.g. cavitation, NPSH, bearing.
